The motivic structures 𝖫𝖲 12 \mathsf{LS}_{12} and 𝖲 16 \mathsf{S}_{16} in the cohomology of moduli spaces of curves Thanks: S.C. was supported by a Hermann-Weyl-Instructorship from the Forschungsinstitut für Mathematik at ETH Zürich. This research was partially conducted during the period H.L served as a Clay Research Fellow. S.P. was supported in part by NSF grants DMS–2053261 and DMS–2302475, and he conducted parts of this research during a visit to the Institute for Advanced Study supported by the Charles Simonyi Endowment. T.W. has been supported by the NCCR SwissMAP, funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation
Samir Canning, Hannah Larson, Sam Payne, Thomas Willwacher

Abstract
. We study the appearances of 𝖫𝖲 12 \mathsf{LS}_{12} and 𝖲 16 \mathsf{S}_{16} in the weight-graded compactly supported cohomology of moduli spaces of curves. As applications, we prove new nonvanishing results for the middle cohomology groups of ℳ 9 \mathcal{M}_{9} and ℳ 11 \mathcal{M}_{11} and give evidence to support the conjecture that dim ℚ H c 2 ​ g + k ​ ( ℳ g ) \dim_{\mathbb{Q}}H^{2g+k}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g}) grows at least exponentially with g g for almost all k k .



1.
Introduction

There are few isomorphism classes of irreducible Hodge structures and
\ell
-adic Galois representations that appear as subquotients of the compactly supported cohomology groups of moduli spaces of smooth and stable curves in motivic weights less than or equal to 15, and these are completely classified in
[
3
,
6
]
, confirming predictions from arithmetic
[
10
]
. It is therefore natural to study these cohomology groups by computing the multiplicities with which each of these irreducible motivic structures appear.

The strategy of studying the cohomology of moduli spaces one motivic structure at a time has already proved fruitful; appearances of the trivial motivic structure in weight zero refuted a longstanding conjecture about the cohomology of
\mathcal{M}_{g}
and established new connections to graph cohomology and Grothendieck-Teichmüller theory
[
8
,
9
]
. Graph complex techniques were then used to study multiplicities of the structures
\mathsf{L}
and
\mathsf{S}_{12}
in weights 2 and 11, respectively, providing many nontrivial new lower bounds on dimensions of cohomology groups of
\mathcal{M}_{g}

[
14
,
15
]
. Further computations of Euler characteristics (alternating sums of multiplicities) of
\mathsf{S}_{12}
and
\mathsf{L}\mathsf{S}_{12}
in weights 11 and 13 were used to prove that
\mathcal{M}_{g}
does not have polynomial point count for
g\geq 9

[
7
]
.

Here we pursue some natural next steps in this program, focusing on
\mathsf{L}\mathsf{S}_{12}
and
\mathsf{S}_{16}
in motivic weights 13 and 15, respectively. Throughout, we consider rational cohomology groups of algebraic varieties and Deligne–Mumford stacks over
\mathbb{Q}
with their associated motivic structures, i.e., a rational mixed Hodge structure and an action of
\Gal(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}|\mathbb{Q})
on the extension of scalars to
\mathbb{Q}_{\ell}
. The structures
\mathsf{L}:=H^{2}(\mathbb{P}^{1})
,
\mathsf{S}_{k+1}:=W_{k}H^{k}(\mathcal{M}_{1,k})
, and
\mathsf{L}\mathsf{S}_{12}:=\mathsf{L}\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}}\mathsf{S}_{12}
play a special role. We say that a cohomology group is of
Tate type
if the associated graded of its weight filtration is a direct sum of tensor powers of
\mathsf{L}
. If
X
is smooth then, by Poincaré duality,
H^{*}(X)
is of Tate type if and only if
H^{*}_{c}(X)
is of Tate type.

1.1.
Weight 13 cohomology

In
[
7
, Section 4]
, we gave a presentation for
H^{13}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})
for all
g
and
n
. Surprisingly, this presentation stabilizes with the genus; it is independent of
g
, for
g\geq 2
. Here, we use this presentation to produce a graph complex that computes
\mathrm{gr}^{W}_{13}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})
and study its cohomology for small
g
and
n
.

Recall that
H^{*}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})
is of Tate type for
3g+2n\leq 24

[
7
, Theorem 1.5]
. Thus
\mathrm{gr}_{k}^{W}H^{*}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})
vanishes when
k
is odd and
3g+2n\leq 24
. We improve this vanishing bound by one for
k=13
.

Proposition 1.1
.

If
3g+2n\leq 25
then
\mathrm{gr}_{13}^{W}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})=0
.

We also compute
\mathrm{gr}^{W}_{13}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})
in the first cases where it does not vanish, when
3g+2n
is
26
or
27
. Let
\delta_{0,n}
denote the Kronecker delta function, i.e.,
\delta_{0,n}=1
if
n=0
and is
0
otherwise. For a partition
\lambda
of a positive integer
n
, let
V_{\lambda}
denote the corresponding Specht module, which is an irreducible representation of
\mathbb{S}_{n}
.

Theorem 1.2
.

Suppose
3g+2n\in\{26,27\}
. Then
\mathrm{gr}_{13}^{W}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})
is nonzero only in degree

k(g,n)=3g+n-2-\delta_{0,n},

and there is an
\mathbb{S}_{n}
-equivariant isomorphism
\mathrm{gr}_{13}^{W}H^{k(g,n)}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})\cong Z_{g,n}\otimes\mathsf{L}\mathsf{S}_{12}
, where

\displaystyle Z_{1,12}

\displaystyle\cong V_{21^{10}}

\displaystyle Z_{2,10}

\displaystyle\cong V_{1^{10}}

\displaystyle Z_{3,9}

\displaystyle\cong V_{1^{9}}

\displaystyle Z_{4,7}

\displaystyle\cong V_{1^{7}}

\displaystyle Z_{5,6}

\displaystyle\cong V_{1^{6}}\oplus V_{21^{4}}^{\oplus 2}

\displaystyle Z_{6,4}

\displaystyle\cong V_{1^{4}}

\displaystyle Z_{7,3}

\displaystyle\cong V_{1^{3}}\oplus V_{21}^{\oplus 2}

\displaystyle Z_{8,1}

\displaystyle\cong\mathbb{Q}

\displaystyle Z_{9,0}

\displaystyle\cong\mathbb{Q}

In particular, we have
\mathrm{gr}_{13}^{W}H^{24}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{9})\cong\mathsf{L}\mathsf{S}_{12}
.

Note that
\mathrm{gr}_{2}^{W}H^{24}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{9})
is also nonzero; the shift of
W_{0}H^{6}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{3})\wedge W_{0}H^{15}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{6})
appearing in the first term of
[
14
, Theorem 1.2]
contributes a summand isomorphic to
\mathsf{L}
.

1.2.
Weight 15 cohomology and appearances of
\mathsf{S}_{16}

Next, we describe the
\mathsf{S}_{16}
-isotypic part of
H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})
. Note that
\mathsf{S}_{16}
is not a subquotient of the cohomology of
\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n}
for
g\neq 1
, by
[
6
, Theorem 1.1]
. Hence, the essential case is when
g=1
. There is a canonical splitting

H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,15})=\mathsf{S}_{16}\oplus V

where
V^{\mathrm{ss}}\cong\bigoplus\mathsf{L}^{2}\mathsf{S}_{12},
by
[
6
, Lemma 8.3]
. The subspace
\mathsf{S}_{16}\subset H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,15})
is the image of

H^{15}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{1,15})\rightarrow H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,15}),

or, equivalently, the kernel of the restriction map
H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,15})\to H^{15}(\partial\mathcal{M}_{1,15})
. The following description of
H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n})
is well-known to experts (cf.
[
12
,
13
]
).

Let
K^{15}_{n}:=V_{(n-14)1^{14}}
denote the
\mathbb{S}_{n}
-representation associated to the hook shape Young diagram of size
n
with 15 boxes in the first column. (For
n<15
, we set
K^{15}_{n}:=0.)

It is an irreducible
\mathbb{S}_{n}
-representation of dimension
\binom{n-1}{14}
generated by elements
k_{P}
, for ordered subsets
P\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}
of size
15
, with relations

(1.1)

k_{\sigma(P)}=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\cdot k_{P},\quad\mbox{and}\quad\sum_{j=0}^{15}(-1)^{j}\cdot k_{\{a_{0},\ldots,\widehat{a_{j}},\ldots,a_{15}\}}=0,

for any permutation
\sigma
of
P
, and any size
16
ordered subset
\{a_{0},\ldots,a_{15}\}\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}
.

Theorem 1.3
.

There is an
\mathbb{S}_{n}
-equivariant direct sum decomposition of the form

H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n})\cong(K^{15}_{n}\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}}\mathsf{S}_{16})\oplus V_{n},

where the underlying motivic structure of the second summand is
V_{n}^{\mathrm{ss}}\cong\bigoplus\mathsf{L}^{2}\mathsf{S}_{12}
.

The isomorphism identifies
(\mathbb{Q}\cdot k_{P})\otimes\mathsf{S}_{16}
with the pullback of
\mathsf{S}_{16}\subset H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,P})
under the forgetful map
\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n}\to\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,P}
.

We now focus on the
\mathsf{S}_{16}
-isotypic subspace of
\mathrm{gr}_{15}^{W}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})
. By Theorem
1.3
, we have a direct sum decomposition of Hodge structures or
\ell
-adic Galois representations

(1.2)

\mathrm{gr}^{W}_{15}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})\cong U_{g,n}\oplus W_{g,n},

where

U_{g,n}^{\mathrm{ss}}\cong\bigoplus\mathsf{S}_{16}\quad\mbox{and}\quad W_{g,n}^{\mathrm{ss}}\cong\bigoplus\mathsf{L}^{2}\mathsf{S}_{12}.

Recall also that
\mathrm{gr}_{15}^{W}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})=0
for
3g+2n\leq 24
, by
[
7
, Theorem 1.5]
.
We have the following improved vanishing result for
U_{g,n}
.

Proposition 1.4
.

If
3g+2n\leq 32
then
U_{g,n}=0
.

In particular, in the key special case where there are no marked points, the motivic structure
\mathsf{S}_{16}
does not appear in
\mathrm{gr}_{15}^{W}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g})
for
g\leq 10
.

Following the usual convention, we omit the second subscript when
n=0
and write
U_{g}:=U_{g,0}
. Let
U^{k}_{g}\subset\mathrm{gr}^{W}_{15}H^{k}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g})
denote the degree
k
part of
U_{g}
.

Theorem 1.5
.

For
g=11
, the
\mathsf{S}_{16}
-isotypic subspace of
\mathrm{gr}^{W}_{15}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{11})
is given by

U_{11}^{k}\cong\begin{cases}\mathsf{S}_{16}&\mbox{ for }k=30,\\
0&\mbox{ otherwise.}\end{cases}

For
g=12
, we have
U_{12}=0
.

Thus, we have shown that the middle cohomology group
H^{30}(\mathcal{M}_{11})
does not vanish, which was not previously known. See §
6
for a complete computation of
U_{g,n}
in the cases where
3g+2n\leq 36
.

Although we do not yet have a complete description of
U_{g}
, e.g., in terms of shifts of symmetric and exterior powers of weight zero cohomology groups of smaller moduli spaces, as in
[
14
, Theorem 1.2]
, we produce a large subspace of this form.

Let
\mathbb{V}_{g}^{r,k}
denote the degree
k
and genus
g
part of the
r
-fold symmetric power

\Sym^{r}\bigg(\bigoplus_{h}W_{0}H_{c}^{*}(\mathcal{M}_{h})\bigg).

Here we follow the Koszul sign convention, so the underlying graded vector space of the symmetric algebra on a graded vector space
U^{*}
is
\Sym^{*}(U^{\mathrm{even}})\otimes\bigwedge^{*}(U^{\mathrm{odd}})
.

Theorem 1.6
.

There is an injective map

(1.3)

\begin{aligned} \big(\mathbb{V}^{14,k-29}_{g-1}\oplus\mathbb{V}^{14,k-30}_{g-2}\oplus\mathbb{V}^{13,k-30}_{g-3}\oplus\mathbb{V}^{10,k-30}_{g-5}\oplus\mathbb{V}^{7,k-30}_{g-7}\oplus\mathbb{V}^{4,k-30}_{g-9}\oplus\mathbb{V}^{1,k-30}_{g-11}\big)\otimes\mathsf{S}_{16}\to U^{k}_{g}.\end{aligned}

The injection we construct comes from a subcomplex of a graph complex that computes
U_{g}
; see §
7
for details. The map (
1.3
) is not surjective; for example,
U_{11}
is not in the image.

Theorem
1.6
yields many new nonvanishing results and lower bounds on the dimensions of cohomology groups of
\mathcal{M}_{g}
. For instance, the exponential growth of
\dim H^{2g+20}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g})
, which was not previously known, is deduced from the summand
\mathbb{V}^{10,k-30}_{g-5}
using the exponential growth of
\dim W_{0}H^{2g}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g})
. We similarly prove exponential growth of
\dim H^{2g+k}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g})
for 20 other values of
k
for which this was not previously known; see Corollary
7.4
.

The following picture illustrates the values of
k
for which
\dim_{\mathbb{Q}}H^{2g+k}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g})
is now known to grow at least exponentially with
k
, with dark gray boxes for the previously known cases (from weight 0, 2 and 11) and light gray boxes for the new contributions from
U_{g}
.

0
10
20
30
40
50
60
70
80

This provides further evidence for the conjecture that
\dim H^{2g+k}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g})
grows at least exponentially with
g
for all but finitely many non-negative integers
k

[
15
, Conjecture 1.3]
. The analogous statement for moduli spaces of principally polarized abelian varieties is a recent theorem: the dimension of
H^{2g+k}_{c}(\mathcal{A}_{g})
grows at least exponentially with
g
for all but finitely many non-negative integers
k

[
4
, Corollary 1.5]
.

Our study of the multiplicity of
\mathsf{S}_{16}
in
\mathrm{gr}_{15}^{W}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})
also leads naturally to a generating function for the corresponding Euler characteristic. See Theorem
8.1
. The result is similar to the generating function for the weight
11
Euler characteristic of
\mathcal{M}_{g,n}
from
[
15
, Section 7]
.

2.
Graph complexes in weight 13

In this section, we define and study graph complexes that compute the weight
13
graded piece of
H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})
. We start with the Getzler–Kapronov graph complex, obtained as the Feynman transform of the modular operad
H^{13}(\overline{\mathcal{M}})
, and then pass to a simpler quasi-isomorphic graph complex whose generators we explicitly describe.

2.1.
Reminder of the Feynman transform

Recall, e.g. from
[
14
, Section 2]
, that the associated graded of the weight filtration

\mathrm{gr}^{W}_{k}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n}):=W_{k}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})/W_{k-1}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})

is identified with the cohomology of the Feynman transform of
H(\overline{\mathcal{M}})
, the modular cooperad whose
(g,n)
part is
H^{*}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})
.
This Feynman transform is also known as the Getzler–Kapranov graph complex and is denoted

(2.1)

\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}\bigg(\bigoplus_{\Gamma\text{ stable graph}}\Big(\bigotimes_{v\in V(\Gamma)}H^{*}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g_{v},n_{v}})\otimes\mathbb{Q}[-1]^{\otimes|E(\Gamma)|}\Big)\bigg)\Big/\sim,

where the sum is over stable graphs of type
(g,n)
. The relations in (
2.1
) are induced by isomorphisms of stable graphs; the end result is isomorphic to a direct sum over representatives of the finitely many isomorphism classes of stable graphs of type
(g,n)
, and the contribution of
[\Gamma]
is the
\Aut(\Gamma)
-coinvariants of the parenthesized expression. The differential is induced by pullback along the tautological clutching and gluing maps.

Each element of
\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}
is represented by a linear combination of stable graphs with
n
numbered legs, such that the sum of the genera
g_{v}
of the vertices plus the first Betti number of the graph is
g
, and such that each vertex
v
of valence
n_{v}
is decorated by an element of
H^{*}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g_{v},n_{v}})
. When each vertex is decorated by a homogeneous element of cohomological degree
k_{v}
, we say that the
weight
of the decorated graph is
k=\sum_{v}k_{v}
.

Let
\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{k}
denote the subspace spanned by generators of weight
k
. The differential preserves these subspaces, giving a direct sum decomposition
\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}\cong\bigoplus_{k}\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{k}
. By construction
\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{k}
is isomorphic to the weight
k
row of the
E_{1}
-page of the weight spectral sequence associated to the inclusion
\mathcal{M}_{g,n}\subset\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n}
.

The differential on
\mathsf{GK}^{k}_{g,n}
has two terms,

d=d_{\vartheta}+d_{\xi}.

The piece
d_{\xi}
acts by creating a self-loop at a vertex

so that the new decoration is the pullback

\sum x^{\prime}\otimes x^{\prime\prime}=\vartheta^{*}x

of
x\in H^{k_{v}}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g_{v},n_{v}})
under the appropriate gluing morphism

\vartheta:\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{h^{\prime},n^{\prime}}\times\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{h^{\prime\prime},n^{\prime\prime}}\to\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g_{v},n_{v}}
.
Here
h^{\prime}+h^{\prime\prime}=g_{v}
and
n^{\prime}+n^{\prime\prime}=n_{v}+2
.
We are interested in the case of weight
k=13
. Since
H^{k^{\prime}}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})=0
for odd
k^{\prime}<11

[
3
]
, generators of
\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{13}
are of the following two forms:

A.

Graphs with one vertex
v
of weight
k_{v}=13
;

B.

Graphs with one vertex
v
of weight
k_{v}=11
and one vertex
u
of weight
k_{u}=2
.

In either case, all other vertices have weight zero.
We also note that a weight 11 vertex must have genus
g_{v}=1
and valence
n_{v}\geq 11
, by
[
5
, Theorem 1.1]
.
Similarly, a weight
13
vertex
w
must have genus
g_{w}\geq 1
and valence
n_{w}\geq 10
by
[
7
, Theorem 1.7]
.

2.2.
Simplifying
\mathsf{GK}^{13}_{g,n}

Next, we simplify the graph complex
\mathsf{GK}^{13}_{g,n}
, following the analogous construction in weight 2
[
14
]
.
We define the graded subspace

\widetilde{I}_{g,n}\subset\mathsf{GK}^{13}_{g,n}

to be the subspace spanned by decorated graphs with one or more of the following features:

(1)

A weight
0
vertex of positive genus.

(2)

A weight
2
vertex
2
of genus
g_{u}\geq 2
.

(3)

A weight
2
vertex of genus
g_{v}=1
and valence
n_{v}\geq 2
, or of genus
g_{v}=1
and valence
n_{v}=1
such that the unique neighbor is a vertex of weight 0.

(4)

A weight 13 vertex
w
of genus
g_{w}\geq 2
.

We also recall that a weight 11 vertex must necessarily have genus
1
for the graph to be a non-zero element of
\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{13}
.
We then define

I_{g,n}:=\widetilde{I}_{g,n}+d\widetilde{I}_{g,n}\subset\mathsf{GK}^{13}_{g,n}

to be the differential closure of
\widetilde{I}_{g,n}
, and we define the quotient complex

\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{13}_{g,n}:=\mathsf{GK}^{13}_{g,n}/I_{g,n}.

The goal is to show the following proposition, to be proven in Section
2.5
below.

Proposition 2.1
.

The projection
\mathsf{GK}^{13}_{g,n}\to\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{13}_{g,n}
is a quasi-isomorphism.

For now, we give a more explicit description of
I_{g,n}
.

Lemma 2.2
.

The subspace
I_{g,n}\subset\mathsf{GK}^{13}_{g,n}
is spanned by decorated graphs possessing at least one of the features (1)–(4) above, together with the following graphs:

(5)

Graphs with a loop attached to a weight 0 vertex.

(6)

Graphs with a loop attached to a weight 2 vertex
u
of genus
g_{u}=0
and decoration in the image of the pullback under the corresponding gluing map
\xi\colon\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}\to\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n_{u}-2}
.

(7)

Linear combinations
(d_{\xi}+d_{\vartheta})\Gamma
, where
\Gamma
has a weight 13 vertex of genus
2
.

Proof.

The subspace
I_{g,n}
is evidently generated by graphs having one the features (1)–(4) above, and elements
d\Gamma
, where
\Gamma
is again such a graph.

First suppose that
\Gamma
has feature (1), i.e., a weight zero vertex
w
of genus
g_{w}\geq 1
.
If
g_{w}>1
, then all terms in
d\Gamma
also have this feature. If
g_{w}=1
, then all terms in
d\Gamma
have this feature, except for one arising from
d_{\xi}\Gamma
, that corresponds to creating a self-loop at
w
and creates feature (5). Thus
d\Gamma
lies in the span of graphs with features (1) and (5). Conversely, given any graph
\Gamma^{\prime}
with feature (5), let
\Gamma
be
be the graph that contracts the self-loop and replaces it with a genus
1
vertex shows. Then
\Gamma^{\prime}
is a term in
d\Gamma
and all other terms have already been shown to lie in
I_{g,n}
, so
\Gamma^{\prime}
is also in
I_{g,n}
.

Next suppose
\Gamma
has feature (2), i.e., a weight 2 vertex
u
of genus
g_{u}\geq 2
. Then any term in
d\Gamma
has a weight 2 vertex of genus
\geq 2
, a weight zero vertex of genus
\geq 1
, or a weight 2 vertex of genus 1 with a self-loop, and hence necessarily of valence
\geq 3
. (Note that one can never have a
(2,0)
vertex because
H^{13}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{2,0})=0
.) Hence
d\Gamma\in\widetilde{I}_{g,n}
.

Next suppose
\Gamma
has feature (3), i.e., a weight 2 vertex
u
of genus 1 as stated.
Then
d_{\vartheta}\Gamma
is a linear combination of terms that again have feature (2) or (1), so that
d_{\vartheta}\Gamma\in\widetilde{I}_{g,n}
. Likewise, the only term in
d_{\xi}\Gamma
that is not readily in
\widetilde{I}_{g,n}
is obtained by creating the self-loop at
u
, giving rise to the graphs having feature (6). Thus,
d\Gamma
lies in the span of graphs with features
(1),(2)
, and
(6)
. Conversely, given a graph
\Gamma^{\prime}
with feature (6), let
\Gamma
be the graph that contracts the self-loop at
u
and decorates the resulting genus
1
vertex with the class guaranteed to pullback to the decoration at
u
. Because
H^{2}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,3})=0
, the vertex
u
must have valence at least
4
; this ensures that the graph
\Gamma
has feature (3). By construction,
\Gamma^{\prime}
is a term in
d\Gamma
and all other terms have already been shown to lie in
I_{g,n}
, so
\Gamma^{\prime}
lies in
I_{g,n}
.

Finally, if
\Gamma
has feature (4) and
g_{v}\geq 3
, then
d\Gamma
is again a linear combination of graphs having features (2) and (4). If
g_{v}=2
, then
d\Gamma
is of type (7).
∎

2.3.
The part of type (12,1)

Each term in the Getzler–Kapranov graph complex comes with an associated
\mathbb{Q}
-Hodge structure, and the differentials respect the Hodge decomposition after tensoring with
\mathbb{C}
. Hence, we have a Hodge decomposition

\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{k}\otimes\mathbb{C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{p,q}.

Specializing to
k=13
, we have

\mathsf{GK}^{13}_{g,n}\otimes\mathbb{C}=\mathsf{GK}^{12,1}_{g,n}\oplus\mathsf{GK}^{1,12}_{g,n},

because the rank 2 Hodge structure
\mathsf{L}\mathsf{S}_{12}
has types
(12,1)
and
(1,12)
.
Similarly,

\displaystyle I_{g,n}\otimes\mathbb{C}

\displaystyle=I_{g,n}^{12,1}\oplus I_{g,n}^{1,12}

\displaystyle\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{13}_{g,n}\otimes\mathbb{C}

\displaystyle=\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n}\oplus\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{1,12}_{g,n},

with
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n}=\mathsf{GK}^{12,1}_{g,n}/I_{g,n}^{12,1}
and
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{1,12}=\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{1,12}/I_{g,n}^{1,12}
.

We introduce graphical notation for generators of
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n}
, following
[
14
,
15
]
.
Generators are decorated graphs, and graphs having features (1)–(7) are set to zero. Because of (1), we may assume that all weight 0 vertices are decorated by
1\in H^{0}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n})
, omit the decoration and genus, and just draw a black vertex.

Similarly, because of (5), we may assume that there are no loops attached to weight zero vertices.
Because of (2), we may assume that all weight
2
vertices have genus
\leq 1
.
The decorations
\delta_{S}
on a weight two vertex of genus zero can be graphically represented by drawing the vertex as two vertices, connected by a special edge

(2.2)

Note that the relations (7
′
) and (7
′′
) allow us to remove all generators from
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{13}
that have a
Z_{B\subset A}
-decorated weight 13 vertex with a self edge
(s,t)
such that
s,t\in A^{c}
. We just need to keep in mind that if
A^{c}=\{s,t\}
these graphs are not zero in
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{13}
, rather they are identified with the right hand term in
(7^{\prime\prime})
.

Proof.

The argument is similar to the proof of Lemma
2.2
, but we must revisit the generators of the form (7). We consider expressions
d\Gamma
where
\Gamma
has a weight 13 vertex
v
of genus 2 decorated with
Z_{B\subset A}
.
The only terms in
d\Gamma

Second,
d_{\vartheta}\Gamma
has terms from splitting
v
into a weight 11 and a weight 2 vertex, each of genus 1.
Because of the genus 1 vertex of weight 2, these terms are of the form (3) above, except in the special case that the new weight 2 vertex has valence 1.
When the new weight
2
vertex has valence
1
, the contribution to
d_{\vartheta}\Gamma
is determined by setting
S=\varnothing
in
[
7
, Lemma 4.5]
. We now consider two cases.

Case 1:
Suppose our starting decoration has
A^{c}\neq\varnothing
. Then the term in
d_{\vartheta}
where the new weight
2
vertex has valence
1

is zero by
[
7
, Lemma 4.5]
. In this case,
the only term in
d\Gamma
not already known to be in
I_{g,n}
is
d_{\xi}\Gamma
, which has the form (7
′
). In this case, the vertex on the right has valence at least
3
because the
A^{c}
for our original decoration was non-empty. Conversely, given a graph
\Gamma^{\prime}
as in (7
′
), contracting the self-loop and replacing it with a genus
1
vertex gives a graph
\Gamma
such that
d\Gamma
is
\Gamma^{\prime}
plus terms already known to be in
I_{g,n}^{12,1}
.

Case 2:
Suppose our starting decoration has
A^{c}=\varnothing
. Then by
[
7
, Lemma 4.5]
, the term in
d_{\vartheta}
in which the new weight
2
vertex has valence
1
is decorated by
-\psi\in H^{2}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,1})
. But in
H^{2}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,1})
, we have
\psi=\frac{1}{12}\delta_{irr}
, by
[
1
, Theorem 2.2]
. This yields the second graph pictured in (7
′′
).
Since
A^{c}=\varnothing
, the first graph pictured in (7
′′
) is

d_{\xi}\Gamma
.
∎

2.4.
One-vertex complex

The proof of Proposition
2.1
will use the spectral sequence on
\mathsf{GK}^{13}_{g,n}
from the filtration by the number of vertices.
To this end, we need to study the one-vertex complexes

V_{g,n}^{k}=\left(H^{k}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})\xrightarrow{\xi^{*}}H^{k}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g-1,n+2})_{\mathbb{S}_{2}}\xrightarrow{\xi^{*}}\cdots\xrightarrow{\xi^{*}}H^{k}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g-h,n+2h})_{\mathbb{S}_{2}\wr\mathbb{S}_{h}}\xrightarrow{\xi^{*}}\cdots\right)

introduced in
[
14
, Section 4]
.
As in loc. cit., the action of the wreath product
\mathbb{S}_{2}\wr\mathbb{S}_{h}=\mathbb{S}_{h}\ltimes\mathbb{S}_{2}^{h}
is understood to include a sign that accounts for the permutation of the tensor factors
\mathbb{Q}[-1]^{\otimes h}
in (
2.1
).
From
[
14
]
we recall the following results on the cohomology:

\displaystyle H^{h}(V_{g,n}^{0})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mathbb{Q}&\text{if $g=h=0$ and $n\geq 3$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

(2.4)

\displaystyle H^{2+h}(V_{g,n}^{2})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}H^{2}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n})&\text{if $g=0$, $h=0$, and $n\geq 4$}\\
\mathbb{Q}\delta_{irr}&\text{if $g=1$, $h=0$, and $n\geq 1$}\\
H^{2}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n+2})_{\mathbb{S}_{2}}/\xi^{*}H^{2}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n})&\text{if $g=1$, $h=1$, and $n\geq 2$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}.

We recall that
H^{2}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n})
is spanned by the classes
\delta_{A}=\delta_{0,A}=\delta_{A^{c}}
for
A\subset\{1,\dots,n\}
, and the subspace
\xi^{*}H^{2}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n})\subset H^{2}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n+2})_{\mathbb{S}_{2}}
is spanned by classes
\delta_{A}
with
\{n+1,n+2\}\subset A
or
\{n+1,n+2\}\subset A^{c}
.

Note that
V_{g,n}^{11}
has at most one non-zero term, and we obtain

H^{11+h}(V^{11}_{g,n})\cong\begin{cases}H^{11}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n+2h})_{\mathbb{S}_{2}\wr\mathbb{S}_{h}}&\text{if $g=h+1$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}.

Lemma 2.4
.

We have

H^{13+h}(V_{g,n}^{13})=\begin{cases}H^{13}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n+2h})_{\mathbb{S}_{2}\wr\mathbb{S}_{h}}/J&\text{if $g=h+1$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

where
J=\xi^{*}H^{13}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{2,n+2h-2})_{\mathbb{S}_{2}\wr\mathbb{S}_{h-1}}
for
h\geq 1
and
J=0
for
h=0
.
Concretely, if we decompose
J\otimes\mathbb{C}=J^{12,1}\oplus J^{1,12}
, then
J^{12,1}
is spanned for
h>0
by the
Z_{B\subset A}
such that
\{s,t\}\subset A^{c}
, where
s,t
correspond to the markings connected by
\xi
.

Proof.

We consider the term of degree
13+h
,

H^{12,1}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g-h,n+2h})_{\mathbb{S}_{2}\wr\mathbb{S}_{h}}

in the complex
V_{g,n}^{12,1}
.
We index the
n+2h
marked points in
\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g-h,n+2h}
by the set

S_{h}:=\{1,\dots,n,s_{1},t_{1},\dots,s_{h},t_{h}\}.

We think of self-edges being present between
s_{j}
and
t_{j}
(for
j=1,\dots,h
).
The coinvariants
H^{12,1}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g-h,n+2h})_{\mathbb{S}_{2}\wr\mathbb{S}_{h}}
is a quotient of

H^{12,1}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g-h,n+2h})
, and is therefore
generated by the images of
Z_{B^{\prime}\subset A^{\prime}}\in H^{12,1}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g-h,n+2h})
with
B^{\prime}\subset A^{\prime}\subset S_{h}
. Below, we identify a subset of these generators that is a basis.

The two endpoints
s_{j},t_{j}
of our self-edges can each be in one of the three disjoint sets
B^{\prime},A^{\prime}\setminus B^{\prime},
or
(A^{\prime})^{c}
.
Accordingly there are 6 different types of such self-edges, of which one (both endpoints in
B^{\prime}
) is zero due to symmetry.

Denote the number of self-edges in the five remaining types by
h_{12},h_{13},h_{22},h_{23}
, and
h_{33}
, where
h_{k\ell}
is the number of self-edges between the
k
th and
\ell
th disjoint sets.
If any of
h_{22},h_{23},
or
h_{33}
is
2
or more, this element vanishes in the space of coinvariants because of the sign for permuting edges.
Let
B\subset A\subset\{1,\dots,n\}
and numbers
h_{22},h_{23},h_{33}\in\{0,1\}
,
h_{12},h_{13}\geq 0
be given such that
h_{12}+h_{13}+h_{22}+h_{23}+h_{33}=h
,
|B|+h_{12}+h_{13}=10
and
2(g-h-1)+|A^{c}|+h_{13}+h_{23}+2h_{33}\geq 2
. Here the last condition ensures that
|(A^{\prime})^{c}|\geq 2
if
g-h-1=0
.
Then we set

\underline{h}=(h_{12},h_{13},h_{22},h_{23},h_{33})\quad\mbox{ and }\quad Z_{B\subset A,\underline{h}}=Z_{B\subset A,h_{12},h_{13},h_{22},h_{23},h_{33}}=Z_{B^{\prime}\subset A^{\prime}},

with
B^{\prime}:=B\sqcup\{s_{1},\dots,s_{h_{12}+h_{13}}\}
and

A^{\prime}:=(A\cup B^{\prime})\sqcup\{t_{1},\dots,t_{h_{12}}\}\sqcup\underbrace{\{s_{h_{12}+h_{13}+1},t_{h_{12}+h_{13}+1}\}}_{\text{if $h_{22}=1$}}\sqcup\{s_{h_{12}+h_{13}+h_{22}+1},\dots,s_{h_{12}+h_{13}+h_{22}+h_{23}}\}.

Then the
Z_{B\subset A,\underline{h}}
form a basis
for
H^{12,1}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g-h,n+2h})_{\mathbb{S}_{2}\wr\mathbb{S}_{h}}

if we require in addition the following condition coming from
[
7
, Lemma 4.11]
:

•

If
|(A^{\prime})^{c}|=2
and
g=h+1
, then
\min((A^{\prime})^{c})\in\{1,\dots,n\}
and
\min(A^{\prime})^{c}<\min(B^{\prime})
, where we order the set
S_{h}=\{1,\dots,n,s_{1},t_{1},\dots,s_{h},t_{h}\}
as indicated.

Note that in the case
A=\{1,\dots,n\}
the element is zero modulo the relations.

In our basis, by
[
7
, Lemma 4.3]
, the differential
\xi^{*}
acts as

\xi^{*}(Z_{B\subset A,h_{12},h_{13},h_{22},h_{23},h_{33}})=\begin{cases}0&\text{if $g=h+1$ or $h_{33}=1$}\\
Z_{B\subset A,h_{12},h_{13},h_{22},h_{23},1}&\text{if $g>h+1$ and $h_{33}=0$.}\end{cases}

The element on the right-hand side (if not
0
) is again a basis element of

H^{12,1}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g-h-1,n+2h+2})_{\mathbb{S}_{2}\wr\mathbb{S}_{h}}\subset V_{g,n}^{12,1}

except when
g=h+2
and
|A^{c}|=h_{13}=h_{23}=h_{33}=0
.
In the latter case we have

(2.5)

Z_{B\subset A,h_{12},h_{13},h_{22},h_{23},1}=\begin{cases}0&\text{if $B=\emptyset$}\\
\pm 2Z_{(B\setminus i)\subset A,h_{12},h_{13}+1,h_{22},h_{23},0}&\text{if $B\neq\emptyset$}\end{cases}

for
i:=\min(B)
, using the genus
1
relations as in
[
7
, Lemma 4.6]
.
Computing cohomology, the basis elements hence cancel in pairs, except for the following:

•

Elements
Z_{B\subset A,h_{12},h_{13},h_{22},h_{23},0}
in the case that
g=h+1
, with
|A^{c}|+h_{13}+h_{23}\geq 3
.

•

Elements

Z_{B\subset A,h_{12},0,h_{22},h_{23},0}
in the case that
g=h+1
, with
A^{c}\neq\emptyset
,
|A^{c}|+h_{23}=2
and
\min(A^{c})<\min(B)
.

In particular, these all live in the top degree
13+g-1
of the complex
V^{13}_{g,n}
so that the result of the lemma follows.
∎

Remark 2.5
.

Note that (
2.5
) in particular implies that the element
Z_{(B\setminus i)\subset A,h_{12},h_{13},h_{22},h_{23},0}
with
h_{13}>0
is trivial in the cohomology of
V^{13}_{g,n}
.

Similarly, consider the definition of
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n}
and Lemma
2.3
above.

\Gamma\in\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n}
be a graph that has a weight 13 vertex of the form

(2.6)

i.e., there is at least one self-edge with one endpoint in
B^{\prime}
, the other in
(A^{\prime})^{c}
, and we have
|(A^{\prime})^{c}|=2
.
The relations in
H^{12,1}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n})
are determined by
[
7
, Lemma 4.6]
(for
n=12
) and the paragraph following it (for
n\geq 12
). Using these relations, we have that

(2.7)

2.5.
Proof of Proposition
2.1

We equip both the domain and target of the projection

\pi\colon\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{13}\to\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{13}/I_{g,n}=:\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{13}

with the descending filtration on the number of vertices in the generating graphs. The associated spectral sequences automatically converge to the cohomologies by finite dimensionality.
Hence it is sufficient to show that the morphism
\pi
induces a quasi-isomorphism on the
E_{1}
-pages of the spectral sequences.
First consider the
E^{0}
-page:
The associated graded differential on
\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{13}
is given by
d_{\xi}
, while on
\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{13}/I_{g,n}
it is zero.
The complex
(\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{13},d_{\xi})
is identified with a sum of direct summands of tensor products of one-vertex complexes. More precisely, we may write

(\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{13},d_{\xi})\cong\Big(\bigoplus_{\Gamma}\otimes_{v\in V(\Gamma)}V_{g_{v},n_{v}}^{k_{v}}\otimes\mathbb{Q}[-1]^{\otimes|E(\Gamma)|}\Big)_{\Aut(\Gamma)}

where the sum is over isomorphism classes of stable graphs without self-loops of genus
g
, with
n
external legs and with weighted vertices of total weight
13
, and the
V_{g_{v},n_{v}}^{k_{v}}
are the one-vertex complexes of the preceding section.
Since taking cohomology commutes with taking coinvariants under finite group actions, as well as sums and tensor products, we find that the
E_{1}
-page of our spectral sequence is

E_{1}:=H(\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{13},d_{\xi})\cong\Big(\bigoplus_{\Gamma}\otimes_{v\in V(\Gamma)}H(V_{g_{v},n_{v}}^{k_{v}})\otimes\mathbb{Q}[-1]^{\otimes|E(\Gamma)|}\Big)_{\Aut(\Gamma)}.

Comparing the cohomologies of the one-vertex complexes
H(V_{g_{v},n_{v}}^{k_{v}})
computed in the previous section with the definition of
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{13}
, we see that the induced map
E_{1}\to\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{13}
is almost an isomorphism. The only difference is that by (
2.4
) the cohomology of
V_{1,m}^{2}
is non-trivial in degree 2 for every
m\geq 1
(represented by
\delta_{irr}
), whereas in the definition of
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{13}
we set all graphs with a genus-1-weight-
2
vertex of valence
\geq 1
or not adjacent to the weight 11 vertex to zero.
To address this difference one proceeds again as in
[
14
]
and considers a second, nested spectral sequence such that the differential on the associated graded splits off the weight 2 vertex and creates a univalent vertex.

2.6.
The differential on
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{12,1}

Recall from Section
2.1
that the differential on
\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}
has two terms
d=d_{\vartheta}+d_{\xi}
.
This differential descends to a differential on the complex
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{12,1}
whose combinatorial form we shall now describe.
First, the piece
d_{\xi}
is zero on
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{12,1}
, essentially by construction.
Graphically the piece
d_{\vartheta}
acts by splitting vertices. We shall describe the action on each type of vertex.

•

Weight 0 vertices: Here
d_{\vartheta}
acts by replacing the vertex with two vertices, summing over all ways of attaching the incident half-edges:

Weight 13 vertex:
It is again helpful to represent the decoration (by
Z_{B\subset A}
, say) at the weight 13 vertex by drawing two vertices connected by a crossed edge.
The action of the differential
d_{\vartheta}
is then determined by the pullback formulas

7
, Lemmas 4.4 and 4.5]

3.
Low excess computations in weight 13

3.1.
Blown-up pictures of graphs

Generators of
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n}
are connected graphs, with exactly one vertex of weight 11 or 13, and for the decoration of this vertex we may use the graphical notation of the previous section.
Here we perform explicit computations of the cohomology of
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n}
for the pairs
(g,n)
such that
3g+2n
is at most 27. In particular, we prove Proposition
1.1
and Theorem
1.2
. To this end, we need to enumerate all contributing graphs, and this is notationally easier if we draw our graphs differently, using the blown-up picture as in
[
14
,
15
]
.
More precisely, for a weight 11 vertex decorated by
\omega_{A}
, we remove the genus
1
vertex, leaving the edges incident to
v
as external legs. Of those, we mark the ones in
A
with a symbol
\omega
and the others by
\epsilon
.

We emphasize that this is merely a different way of drawing graphs.
Furthermore, we remind the reader that due to the relations on the decorations, our graph complex
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n}
is not fully combinatorial, i.e., there are relations between some graphs.

3.2.
Excess

We define the excess

E(g,n):=3g+2n-25.

We will compute the cohomology of
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n}
for all pairs
g,n
such that
E(g,n)\leq 2
.

To this end, let us write each generator
\Gamma
of
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n}
as a union of its blown-up components:

\Gamma=C_{1}\cup\cdots\cup C_{k}.

Let
g_{i}
be the contribution of
C_{i}
to the genus of
\Gamma
. More precisely,

g_{i}=h^{1}(C_{i})+\#\epsilon+\#\omega-1,

i.e., the loop order of
C_{i}
plus the number of its
\epsilon
and
\omega
labeled legs minus one. Then we define the excess of
C_{i}
as

(3.1)

E(C_{i}):=3g_{i}+2n_{i}-2\#\omega=3h^{1}(C_{i})+3\#\epsilon+\#\omega+2n_{i}-3.

Lemma 3.1
.

The excess is additive over blown-up components, in the sense that for any graph
\Gamma=C_{1}\cup\cdots\cup C_{k}\in\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n}
we have

(3.2)

E(g,n)=E(C_{1})+\cdots+E(C_{k}),

and the excess of each blown-up component is non-negative.

Proof.

For the first statement note that
g=1+\sum_{i=1}^{k}g_{i}
, and the total number of
\omega
-legs must be 11.
The second statement follows as in
[
15
, Lemma 4.2]
.
∎

The excess provides a measure of the combinatorial complexity of the relevant graphs. In particular, the additivity property of the above lemma helps us
to organize our calculations. By enumerating all blown up components of low excess, it becomes possible to compute
H^{k}(\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n})
by hand for all
g,n
with
E(g,n)\leq 2
.

Excess 0 and proof of Proposition

3.1
) and are hence easily seen to be one of the following forms:

Using the conventions introduced in §
2.3
,
each generator of
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n}
must have exactly one marked edge.
Graphs with the third component in the list above are however zero in
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n}
by (
2.8
).
This means that every generator
\Gamma\in\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n}
must have a blown-up component of excess at least one, and we arrive at the following corollary of Lemma
3.1
, that is also stated as Proposition
1.1
in the introduction.

Corollary 3.2
.

If
E(g,n)<1
then
\mathrm{gr}^{W}_{13}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})=0.

3.4.
Excess 1

We next consider the case of excess one. In this case generators of
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n}
must be unions of blown-up components of excess zero as above, and one blown-up component of excess one, containing a crossed edge.
The combinatorially possible excess 1 components with a crossed edge are:

In each case, the total number of
\omega
-legs must be 11.
Note that the graphs
\Gamma^{(0)}_{\delta}
and
\Gamma^{(0)}_{s}
only exist in genera
g\geq 4
. When
g\geq 4
and
n
is such that
3g+2n=26
, the three graphs above form a basis of
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n}
. In genus
2
, we have that
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{2,10}
is one-dimensional, spanned by
\Gamma^{(0)}_{irr}
.

The cohomological degree of the graphs
\Gamma^{(0)}_{irr}
and
\Gamma^{(0)}_{\delta}
above is
k=24-n
, while that of
\Gamma^{(0)}_{s}
is
k=23-n
.
Using (
2.11
),
one checks that the differential sends
\Gamma^{(0)}_{s}
to a non-zero multiple of
\Gamma^{(0)}_{\delta}
plus a multiple of
\Gamma^{(0)}_{irr}
. Note that of the six terms in (
2.11
) only the the third and the fifth term contribute, with the third term producing a multiple of
\Gamma^{(0)}_{irr}
(after using the relation (
2.7
)), and the fifth term producing
-\Gamma^{(0)}_{\delta}
(after replacing the
\psi
class with a boundary class). In particular, the first term in the second line of (
2.11
) is zero in this case because there cannot be a weight 13 vertex of genus 1 and valence 11.
In the end, we retain only one-dimensional cohomology, generated by
\Gamma^{(0)}_{irr}
. We hence obtain:

\displaystyle H^{k}(\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{2,10})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{1^{10}}&\text{for $k=14$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{4,7})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{1^{7}}&\text{for $k=17$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{6,4})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{1^{4}}&\text{for $k=20$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{8,1})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{1}&\text{for $k=23$}\\
0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

3.5.
Excess 2

A general generator
\Gamma
of
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n}
in excess 2 can have either two blown-up components of excess one each, or one component of excess 2, necessarily with a crossed edge.
As in
[
15
, Section 4.2]
, the relevant excess one components without crossed edge are

\displaystyle\mapsto 0

Note that the generators
\Gamma_{ij}^{(2)}
,
\Gamma_{i}^{(2)}
are not independent; there are relations from the weight 13 relations, depending on the genus.
If
g=1
, only
\Gamma_{ij}^{(2)}
contributes, and modulo relations the contribution is the irreducible representation
V_{21^{n-2}}
.
If
g\geq 3
and
n\geq 2
, the
\Gamma^{(2)}_{i}
are linearly independent, the
\Gamma_{ij}^{(2)}
can be expressed through the
\Gamma^{(2)}_{i}
, and the overall
\mathbb{S}_{n}
-representation is
V_{1^{n}}\oplus V_{21^{n-2}}
.

24-n

We can now compute the cohomology of
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n}
for
3g+2n=27
. The complex is concentrated in degrees
23-n
,
24-n
,
25-n
. Note that some generators exist only for higher genus or higher
n
. There is no cocycle of degree
23-n
, since the image of the differential is of full dimension. This is seen already by looking only at the leading terms
\Gamma_{b\overline{4}}^{(2)}
,
\Gamma_{\epsilon\overline{b}}^{(2)}
,
\Gamma_{\overline{B}^{\prime}}^{(2)}
.
Note that these generators only exist for
g
large enough, i.e.,
g\geq 4
or
g\geq 7
respectively. But if they do not (because
g
is too small), the same holds for the corresponding generators of degree
23-n
.
Hence we conclude that
H^{23-n}(\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n})=0
for all
g,n
considered.

Next we consider cocycles
x
of degree
24-n
.
The general cocycle is a linear combination of the
9
generators in degree
24-n
. By adding an exact term to
x
we may however assume that this linear combination does not involve
\Gamma_{b\overline{4}}^{(2)}
,
\Gamma_{\epsilon\overline{b}}^{(2)}
,
\Gamma_{\overline{B}^{\prime}}^{(2)}
.
Assume first that
n\geq 1
. Then we claim that no linear combination of the remaining generators can be closed. This is so because the image of the generators under the differential is already of full rank if projected to the subspace spanned by the “leading terms”
\Gamma_{birr}^{(2)}
,
\Gamma_{b\overline{b}}^{(2)}
,

\Gamma_{j\overline{b}}^{(2)}
,

\Gamma_{j,irr}^{(2)}
,

\Gamma_{\overline{b}\overline{b}}^{(2)}
,

\Gamma_{\overline{b}i}^{(2)}
.
Hence we have
H^{24-n}(\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{g,n})=0
for
n\geq 1
.
In the special case
n=0
, i.e.,
g=9
, the generator
\Gamma_{j,irr}^{(2)}
of degree
25
does not exist, while
\Gamma_{\epsilon,irr}^{(2)}
does exist.
Hence a linear combination of
\Gamma_{\epsilon,irr}^{(2)}
and
\Gamma_{4irr}^{(2)}
is a cocycle, so that
H^{24}(\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{9,0})
is one-dimensional.

Finally, we consider degree
25-n
.
Any element
x
of that degree is a cocyle.
By adding exact terms we may ensure that
x
does not involve the generators

\Gamma_{birr}^{(2)}
,

\Gamma_{b\overline{b}}^{(2)}
,

\Gamma_{j\overline{b}}^{(2)}
,

\Gamma_{\overline{b}\overline{b}}^{(2)}
,

\Gamma_{\overline{b}i}^{(2)}
,
and in addition we have to mod out the linear combination
\sum_{j}\pm\Gamma_{j,irr}^{(2)}
(for
g>1
,
n>0
), that accounts for one copy of the sign representation
V_{1^{n}}
of
\mathbb{S}_{n}
.
Our
x
can hence be a linear combination of the generators
\Gamma_{i}^{(2)}
,

\Gamma_{j,irr}^{(2)}
and
\Gamma_{ij}^{(2)}
.
The generators
\Gamma_{i}^{(2)}
exist for
g\geq 3
and
n\geq 1
and contribute the representation
V_{1^{n}}\oplus V_{21^{n-2}}
of
\mathbb{S}_{n}
.
As explained above the generators
\Gamma_{j,irr}^{(2)}
and
\Gamma_{ij}^{(2)}
in total contribute an
\mathbb{S}_{n}
representation
V_{21^{n-2}}
if
g=1
, and a representation
V_{1^{n}}\oplus V_{21^{n-2}}
for
g>1
,
n>0
. As mentioned above, in the case
g>1
we have to remove the
V_{1^{n}}
again (since it is in the image of the differential).
Hence we arrive at the following cohomology table:

\displaystyle H^{k}(\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{1,12})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{21^{10}}&\text{for $k=13$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{3,9})

\displaystyle=\scalebox{.95}{$\begin{cases}V_{1^{9}}\oplus V_{21^{7}}\oplus V_{21^{7}}&\text{for $k=16$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}$
}

\displaystyle H^{k}(\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{5,6})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{1^{6}}\oplus V_{21^{4}}\oplus V_{21^{4}}&\text{for $k=19$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{7,3})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{1^{3}}\oplus V_{21}\oplus V_{21}&\text{for $k=22$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{12,1}_{9,0})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mathbb{C}&\text{for $k=24$}\\
0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

This completes the proof of Theorem
1.2
.

4.
The
\mathsf{S}_{16}
-isotypic part of
H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})

In this section, we prove Theorem
1.3
, describing the
\mathsf{S}_{16}
-isotypic part of
H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})
. By
[
6
, Theorem 1.1]
, the
\mathsf{S}_{16}
-isotypic part of
H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})
vanishes for
g\geq 2
. Moreover,
H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n})=0
for all
n
. It remains to consider the case
g=1
.

Proof of Theorem
1.3
.

By the argument in
[
7
, Section 4.1]
, it suffices to work in the category of Hodge structures. We have a right exact sequence of Hodge structures

H^{13}(\widetilde{\partial\mathcal{M}_{1,n}})\xrightarrow{\alpha}H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n})\rightarrow W_{15}H^{15}(\mathcal{M}_{1,n})\rightarrow 0,

where the first morphism
\alpha
is of Hodge type
(1,1)
. The image of
\alpha
is therefore disjoint from
H^{15,0}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n})\oplus H^{0,15}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n})
. Because
\mathsf{S}_{16}\otimes\mathbb{C}
is of Hodge type
(15,0),(0,15)
, it follows that the
\mathsf{S}_{16}
-isotypic parts of
W_{15}H^{15}(\mathcal{M}_{1,n})
and
H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n})
agree. By
[
6
, Proposition 2.2]
,

W_{15}H^{15}(\mathcal{M}_{1,n})\cong K^{15}_{n}\otimes\mathsf{S}_{16}
.
∎

Remark 4.1
.

Essentially the same argument shows that the
\mathsf{S}_{k+1}
-isotypic part of
H^{k}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n})
is
K^{k}_{n}\otimes\mathsf{S}_{k+1}
. For odd
k\geq 17
and
g\geq 2
, the
\mathsf{S}_{k+1}
-isotypic part of
H^{k}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})
is not well understood. For example, it is known that the
\mathsf{S}_{18}
-isotypic part of
H^{17}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{2,14})
is nontrivial in the category of
\ell
-adic Galois representations, by
[
16
]
. On the automorphic side of the Langlands correspondence, this corresponds to a Saito–Kurokawa lift of the cusp form
\omega
of level 1 and weight 18 from
\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{Z})
to
\Sp_{4}(\mathbb{Z})
, via relations between the cohomology of
\mathcal{M}_{2,n}
and that of local systems on
\mathcal{A}_{2}
.
This cusp form
\omega
can also be used to construct an explicit holomorphic
17
-form on
\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{2,14}

[
11
, Section 3.5]
, and hence the real Hodge structure
\mathsf{S}_{18}\otimes\overline{\mathcal{R}}
appears in
H^{17}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{2,14})
. However, it is an open problem to show that the rational Hodge structure
\mathsf{S}_{18}
appears in the cohomology of
\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{2,14}
. Moreover, it is unknown (in both Hodge structures and
\ell
-adic Galois representations) whether the
\mathsf{S}_{18}
-isotypic part of
H^{17}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})
is non-zero in any case where
g\geq 3
.

For subsequent calculations, we write an explicit basis for
H^{15,0}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n})
. A weight
16
cusp form
\omega_{15}
for
\SL_{2}(\mathbb{Z})
is a generator for
H^{15,0}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,15})
, on which
\mathbb{S}_{15}
acts by the sign representation
[
2
]
. Let
A\subset\{1,\dots,n\}
be an ordered subset of size
15
. For each such
A
, we have a forgetful map

f_{A}\colon\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n}\rightarrow\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,A},

and we define
\omega_{A}:=f_{A}^{*}\omega_{15}
. Following exactly the same argument as in
[
5
, Section 2.3]
, one can show that the set of forms

\{\omega_{A}:1\in A,A\text{ increasing}\}
forms a basis for
H^{15,0}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n})
. To each such subset
A
, we associate the tableau
T_{A}
of shape
(n-14,1^{14})
with symbols of
A
in order down the first column and the rest of the first row filled in increasing order. The isomorphism
H^{15,0}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n})\rightarrow V_{(n-14)1^{14}}=K_{n}^{15}
sends
\omega_{A}
to the Specht module generator associated to
T_{A}
.

5.
Graph complexes for
\mathcal{M}_{g,n}
in type (15,0)

In this section, we briefly describe
how, in a manner similar to
[
15
]
,
one can construct complexes
B_{g,n}^{15}
and
C_{g,n}^{15}
whose cohomology computes the type
(15,0)
part of
H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})
.
The only difference between the complexes we describe here and the complexes in
[
15
]

is that the truncation happens at 15 marked half-edges.

5.1.
Graph complexes

As discussed in Section
2.3
, above, the cohomology operad
H(\overline{\mathcal{M}})
carries a pure Hodge structure that induces a decomposition of the Feynman transform

\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{k}\otimes\mathbb{C}\cong\bigoplus_{p+q=k}\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{p,q}.

The type
(15,0)
part
\mathsf{GK}^{15,0}_{g,n}
computes the corresponding part of the weight-graded compactly supported cohomology of
\mathcal{M}_{g,n}

H^{*}(\mathsf{GK}^{15,0}_{g,n})\cong\mathrm{gr}_{15,0}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n}):=\mathrm{gr}_{F}^{15}\mathrm{gr}^{W}_{15}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n},\mathbb{C}).

Here,
F
denotes the Hodge filtration in the mixed Hodge structure. In other words, the graph complex
\mathsf{GK}^{15,0}_{g,n}
computes the type
(15,0)
part of the pure Hodge structure
\mathrm{gr}_{15}^{W}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})
.
The generators of
\mathsf{GK}^{15,0}_{g,n}
are stable graphs with
n
external legs, with one special vertex
v
of genus 1 decorated by an element of
H^{15,0}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n_{v}})
. All other vertices
w
are decorated by an element of
H^{0}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g_{w},n_{w}})
, and since this vector space is one-dimensional, we will tacitly assume that they are decorated by 1 and omit the decoration from further discussion.
Recall the explicit description of
H^{15,0}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n_{v}})
of Theorem
1.3
.
Graphically, we may denote the decoration
\omega_{A}\in H^{15,0}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n_{v}})
by marking the 15 half-edges in
A
by arrows.

\scriptscriptstyle\vdots
A

Furthermore, we define the graded subspace

I_{g,n}^{15,0}\subset\mathsf{GK}^{15,0}_{g,n}

spanned by graphs that have either a self-loop at a weight 0 vertex or a weight 0 vertex of positive genus. The subspace
I_{g,n}^{15,0}
is evidently closed under the differential,
dI_{g,n}^{15,0}\subset I_{g,n}^{15,0}
, so that we may consider the quotient complex

\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{15,0}_{g,n}:=\mathsf{GK}^{15,0}_{g,n}/I_{g,n}^{15,0}.

Lemma 5.1
.

The projection to the quotient
\mathsf{GK}^{15,0}_{g,n}\to\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{15,0}_{g,n}
is a quasi-isomorphism.

Proof.

The proof is identical to that of
[
15
, Proposition 3.2]
.
∎

To go further, recall from
[
15
, Section 3.1]
the definition of the auxiliary graph complex
X_{g,n}
.
Generators of
X_{g,n}
are graphs with one special vertex with an arbitrary subset of marked incident half-edges.
The differential is given by splitting vertices, and removing a half-edge from the set of marked half-edges. The complex
X_{g,n}
is acyclic, i.e.,
H(X_{g,n})=0
, see
[
15
, Lemma 3.4]
.
We define the subcomplex

X_{g,n}^{\leq r}\subset X_{g,n}

spanned by graphs such that the number of marked half-edges is
\leq r
.
We then define

(5.1)

\displaystyle C_{g,n}^{15}

\displaystyle:=X_{g,n}^{\leq 14}[-29]

(5.2)

\displaystyle B_{g,n}^{15}

\displaystyle:=\bigg(X_{g,n}/X_{g,n}^{\leq 14}\bigg)[-30].

By acyclicity of
X_{g,n}
we have that

(5.3)

H(B_{g,n}^{15})\cong H(C_{g,n}^{15}),

and the isomorphism is the connecting homomorphism in the natural long exact cohomology sequence associated to the short exact sequence

(5.4)

0\to X_{g,n}^{\leq 14}\to X_{g,n}\to X_{g,n}/X_{g,n}^{\leq 14}\to 0.

There is a natural morphism of dg vector spaces

B_{g,n}^{15}\to\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{15,0}

defined on generators by sending a graph to itself. See
[
15
, Definition 3.5ff.]
for the analogous construction in weight 11, which differs only in the replacement of the truncation constant 14 by 10.

Proposition 5.2
.

The morphism
B_{g,n}^{15}\to\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{15,0}
is a quasi-isomorphism. In particular,

\mathrm{gr}_{15,0}H_{c}^{*}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})\cong H^{*}(B_{g,n}^{15})\cong H^{*}(C_{g,n}^{15}).

Proof.

The proof is identical to the proof of
[
15
, Proposition 3.6]
.
∎

In what follows, we will again draw graphs in the “blown-up” picture, removing the special vertex
v
so that the half-edges incident at
v
become external legs. The legs corresponding to marked half-edges will be marked by a symbol
\omega
, and the non-marked half-edges by a symbol
\epsilon
. See
[
15
, Section 3.2]
or Section
3.1
, above.

6.
Low excess computations in type (15,0)

We define the excess of a generator
\Gamma
of
X_{g,n}
to be

E(\Gamma)=3(g-1)+2n-2\#\omega,

where
\#\omega
is the number of
\omega
-legs of
\Gamma
.
We also define

E^{\prime}(g,n):=3g+2n-33.

Any generator
\Gamma
for
B^{15}_{g,n}
has
\#\omega\geq 15
, and hence

E(\Gamma)\leq E^{\prime}(g,n).

Furthermore
E(\Gamma)\equiv E^{\prime}(g,n)\mod 2
.

Write each generator
\Gamma
for
B^{15}_{g,n}
as a union of its blown-up components:

\Gamma=C_{1}\cup\cdots\cup C_{k}.

The excess is additive

E(\Gamma)=E(C_{1}\cup\cdots\cup C_{k})=E(C_{1})+\cdots+E(C_{k}),

if we continue to define the excess of components by (
3.1
).
As in
[
15
, Lemma 4.2]
, the excess of all generators of
B^{15}_{g,n}
is non-negative.
Hence, we obtain the following result, stated as Proposition
1.4
in the introduction.

Corollary 6.1
.

If
E^{\prime}(g,n)<0
then
\mathrm{gr}_{15,0}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})=0.

The low-excess computations of
[
15
, Section 4]
in weight 11 carry over almost unaltered to the type
(15,0)
situation.
We hence only briefly recall the arguments and state the results, leaving details to loc. cit.

6.1.
Case
E^{\prime}(g,n)=0

E^{\prime}(g,n)=0
, the generators of
B_{g,n}
have the following form:

Note that there are
n

(\omega-j)
-edges and
\frac{g-1}{2}
tripods with three
\omega
-legs each.
The cohomological degree of such a generator is
k=15+\frac{3}{2}(g-1)
.

One hence arrives at the following list of cases in which
\mathrm{gr}_{15,0}H_{c}^{k}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})
is concentrated in a single degree
k
. The
\mathbb{S}_{n}
-action is by the sign representation in each case.

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{1,15})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{1^{15}}&\text{for $k=15$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{3,12})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{1^{12}}&\text{for $k=18$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{5,9})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{1^{9}}&\text{for $k=21$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{7,6})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{1^{6}}&\text{for $k=24$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{9,3})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{1^{3}}&\text{for $k=27$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{11,0})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mathbb{Q}&\text{for $k=30$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

Note, in particular, that the computation for
B^{15}_{11,0}
proves the first statement in Theorem
1.5
.

with the understanding that there is no
(\omega-j)
-edge in
\Gamma^{(1)}_{j}
.
The differential sends
\Gamma^{(1)}
to the alternating sum of
\Gamma_{j}^{(1)}
.
Hence the cohomology of
B^{15}_{g,n}
is the irreducible
\mathbb{S}_{n}
-representation
V_{21^{n-2}}
in degree
k=14+\frac{3}{2}g
, represented by linear combinations of the
\Gamma_{j}^{(1)}
.
We obtain:

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{2,14})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{21^{12}}&\text{for $k=17$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{4,11})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{21^{9}}&\text{for $k=20$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{6,8})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{21^{6}}&\text{for $k=23$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{8,5})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{21^{3}}&\text{for $k=26$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{10,2})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{2}&\text{for $k=29$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}.

After killing terms involving trees with at least 4 leaves, the differential maps
\Gamma^{(2)}_{\epsilon}
,
\Gamma^{(2)}_{ij}
, and
\Gamma^{(2)}_{i;j}
to
0
. On the remaining generators, it is given by:

\displaystyle\Gamma^{(0)}

\displaystyle\mapsto\sum_{j}\pm\Gamma^{(2)}_{\epsilon j}+(const)\Gamma^{(2)}_{\epsilon}

\displaystyle\Gamma^{(2)}_{\epsilon j}

\displaystyle\mapsto\sum_{i}\pm\Gamma^{(2)}_{ij}

\displaystyle\Gamma^{(2)}_{\omega\epsilon\omega\epsilon}

\displaystyle\mapsto\pm\Gamma^{(2)}_{\epsilon}+\sum_{j}\pm\Gamma^{(2)}_{\omega\epsilon j}

\displaystyle\Gamma^{(2)}_{\omega\epsilon j}

\displaystyle\mapsto\sum_{i}\pm\Gamma^{(2)}_{i;j}.

Here one needs to take care that when
n=1
or
g=1
, some of these generators are absent. More precisely, the generators
\Gamma^{(2)}_{ij}
and
\Gamma^{(2)}_{i;j}
are not present when
n=1
, nor are
\Gamma^{(2)}_{i;j}
,
\Gamma^{(2)}_{\omega\epsilon\omega\epsilon}
,
\Gamma^{(2)}_{\omega\epsilon j}
when
g=1
. When all of the generators are present, the cohomology consists of one copy of the sign representation
V_{1^{n}}
of
\mathbb{S}_{n}
, represented by
\Gamma^{(2)}_{\epsilon}+\cdots
, and two copies of the irreducible representation
V_{31^{n-3}}
, represented by linear combinations of graphs of the form
\Gamma^{(2)}_{ij}
and
\Gamma^{(2)}_{i;j}
respectively.
Taking into account the special cases
n=1
and
g=1
, we arrive at the following:

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{1,16})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{31^{13}}&\text{for $k=16$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{3,13})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{1^{13}}&\text{for $k=18$}\\
V_{31^{10}}\oplus V_{31^{10}}&\text{for $k=19$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{5,10})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{1^{1}0}&\text{for $k=21$}\\
V_{31^{7}}\oplus V_{31^{7}}&\text{for $k=22$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{7,7})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{1^{7}}&\text{for $k=24$}\\
V_{31^{4}}\oplus V_{31^{4}}&\text{for $k=25$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{9,4})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{1^{4}}&\text{for $k=27$}\\
V_{31}\oplus V_{31}&\text{for $k=28$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{11,1})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{1}&\text{for $k=30$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}.

6.4.
Case
E^{\prime}(g,n)=3

In the case
E^{\prime}(g,n)=3
the computation is slightly more complex, due to the increase in the number of generators. Proceeding as in
[
15
, Section 4.4]
we obtain:

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{2,15})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{41^{7}}\oplus V_{321^{6}}\oplus V_{31^{8}}&\text{for $k=18$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{4,12})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{21^{10}}&\text{for $k=20$}\\
V_{41^{8}}\oplus V_{41^{8}}\oplus V_{321^{7}}\oplus V_{31^{9}}&\text{for $k=21$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{6,9})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{21^{7}}&\text{for $k=23$}\\
V_{41^{5}}\oplus V_{41^{5}}\oplus V_{321^{4}}\oplus V_{31^{6}}&\text{for $k=24$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{8,6})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{21^{4}}&\text{for $k=26$}\\
V_{41^{5}}\oplus V_{41^{5}}\oplus V_{321}\oplus V_{31^{3}}&\text{for $k=27$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{10,3})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{21}&\text{for $k=29$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle H^{k}(B^{15}_{12,0})

\displaystyle=0

The computation for
B^{15}_{12,0}
completes the proof of Theorem
1.5
.

7.
Infinite families of cohomology classes in
H^{(15,0)}(\mathcal{M}_{g})

We now restrict attention to the special case of
n=0
, allowing the genus
g
to be arbitrarily large. We abbreviate:

\displaystyle B_{g}^{15}

\displaystyle:=B_{g,0}^{15},

\displaystyle C_{g}^{15}

\displaystyle:=C_{g,0}^{15}.

Let
\mathsf{GC}_{0}
be the graph complex generated by connected graphs without self-loops in which every vertex has valence at least
3
. Each generator is given an orientation by a total ordering of the edges. The cohomological degree of a generator is the number of edges. Isomorphic graphs are identified, and two orientations are identified up to sign. The differential acts by splitting vertices. Therefore, the differential preserves the loop order, and we write
\mathsf{GC}_{0}^{(g)}
for the part of loop order
g
.

Analogously to
[
15
, Theorems 5.1 and 6.1]
one shows the following theorems.

Theorem 7.1
.

There is a map of complexes

F\colon\Sym^{14}(\mathsf{GC}_{0})^{(g-1)}[-29]\oplus\Sym^{14}(\mathsf{GC}_{0})^{(g-2)}[-30]\to C_{g}^{15}

that induces an injective map on the level of cohomology

H^{k-29}(\Sym^{14}(\mathsf{GC}_{0})^{(g-1)})\oplus H^{k-30}(\Sym^{14}(\mathsf{GC}_{0})^{(g-2)})\to H^{k}(C_{g}^{15}).

Idea of proof.

The result is shown by the same argument as
[
15
, Theorem 5.1]
, replacing the constant 11 by 15.
We do not reproduce the full proof here, but instead indicate the main underlying ideas.
The generators of
C_{g}^{15}
can be represented by blown-up graphs so that 0–14 of the external legs are labeled by a symbol
\omega
, and the other external legs are labeled by a symbol
\epsilon
. The differential splits into three pieces
\delta=\delta_{s}^{\bullet}+\delta_{s}^{\circ}+\delta_{\omega}
, with
\delta_{s}^{\bullet}
splitting a vertex and
\delta_{s}^{\circ}
fusing some
\epsilon
-legs and at most one
\omega
-leg into a new vertex, while
\delta_{\omega}
replaces one
\omega
at a leg by
\epsilon
.
We also write
\delta_{s}:=\delta_{s}^{\bullet}+\delta_{s}^{\circ}
.

Now consider a cocycle
x\in C_{g}^{15}
and decompose it as

x=x_{0}+\cdots+x_{14},

where
x_{j}
is the part with
j
many
\omega
-legs.
Then the cocycle condition
\delta x=0
implies that
x_{14}
is a cocycle in the complex
(C_{g}^{15},\delta_{s})
, i.e.,
\delta_{s}x_{14}=0
.
Furthermore, if
x_{14}
is not exact in
(C_{g}^{15},\delta_{s})
, then
x
cannot be exact in
(C_{g}^{15},\delta_{s}+\delta_{\omega})
,
so we have constructed a non-trivial cohomology class as desired.

Next, suppose we have graph cocycles
\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{14}\in\mathsf{GC}_{0}
. Then we may build a cocycle

by attaching
\omega
-legs to
\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{14}
and taking the union of the resulting graphs.
This assignment produces a morphism of complexes
\Sym^{14}(\mathsf{GC}_{0})^{(g-1)}[-29]\to(C_{g}^{15},\delta_{s})
.
It is shown in
[
15
]
that this assignment has the following properties.

(1)

It is an injection on homology. This can essentially be deduced by an earlier result of Turchin and the fourth author
[
17
]
, see also the Appendix of
[
15
]
.

(2)

It extends to a morphism of complexes
\Sym^{14}(\mathsf{GC}_{0})^{(g-1)}[-29]\to(C_{g}^{15},\delta)
. The extension involves explicit combinatorial expressions (that are tedious to define) for the missing pieces
x_{13},x_{12},\dots
of our cocycle
x
above.

By our consideration above, this shows that we have an embedding in cohomology

\Sym^{14}(H(\mathsf{GC}_{0}))^{(g-1)}[-29]\to H(C_{g}^{15},\delta).

The embedding of the second summand
\Sym^{14}(H(\mathsf{GC}_{0}))^{(g-2)}[-30]
is shown similarly, except that one adds an additional
\epsilon
-
\epsilon
-edge (in the appropriate way) to the leading order term
x_{14}
, increasing the genus and degree by one.
∎

Theorem 7.2
.

There is a
map of dg vector spaces

E\colon\Sym^{13}(\mathsf{GC}_{0})^{(g-3)}[-30]\oplus\Sym^{10}(\mathsf{GC}_{0})^{(g-5)}[-30]\oplus\Sym^{7}(\mathsf{GC}_{0})^{(g-7)}[-30]\\
\oplus\Sym^{4}(\mathsf{GC}_{0})^{(g-9)}[-30]\oplus\mathsf{GC}_{0}^{(g-11)}[-30]\to B_{g}^{15}

that gives rise to an injective
map on cohomology

E\colon H^{k-30}(\Sym^{13}(\mathsf{GC}_{0}))^{(g-3)}\oplus H^{k-30}(\Sym^{10}(\mathsf{GC}_{0}))^{(g-5)}\oplus H^{k-30}(\Sym^{7}(\mathsf{GC}_{0}))^{(g-7)}\\

Since
y_{16}
has precisely 16
\omega
-legs, this restricts the possible
r
to the set
\{1,4,7,10,13\}
.
The element
y_{16}
satisfies
\delta_{s}y_{16}=0
, but generally
\delta_{\omega}y_{16}\neq 0
.
However, as seen in
[
15
]
, one may define explicitly a cochain
y_{15}\in B_{g}^{15}
with
15

\omega
-legs such that
(\delta_{s}+\delta_{\omega})(y_{15}+y_{16})=0
, so that
y=y_{15}+y_{16}
is a cocycle in
(B_{g}^{15},\delta)
. This construction defines the map
E
of the theorem.

To check the theorem, one (essentially) has to verify that our cocycle
y
is not exact. To this end we may consider its image
x:=\delta_{\omega}y\in C_{g}^{15}
in the complex
C_{g}^{15}
(see (
5.3
), (
5.4
)), and then check that
x
defines a non-trivial cohomology class in the same way as we did in the proof of Theorem
7.1
.
In fact, it turns out that
x
has the form

The leading order term displayed above represents a non-trivial cohomology class in

One furthermore verifies that the images of the injections of Theorems
7.1
and
7.2
are linearly independent inside
\mathrm{gr}^{W}_{15}H^{k}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g})
, just as in
[
15
, Section 6.4]
.

Corollary 7.3
.

There is an injection

\big(H^{k-29}(\Sym^{14}(\mathsf{GC}_{0})^{(g-1)})\oplus H^{k-30}(\Sym^{14}(\mathsf{GC}_{0})^{(g-2)})\oplus H^{k-30}(\Sym^{13}(\mathsf{GC}_{0}))^{(g-3)}\\
\oplus H^{k-30}(\Sym^{10}(\mathsf{GC}_{0}))^{(g-5)}\oplus H^{k-30}(\Sym^{7}(\mathsf{GC}_{0}))^{(g-7)}\oplus H^{k-30}(\Sym^{4}(\mathsf{GC}_{0}))^{(g-9)}\\
\oplus H^{k-30}(\mathsf{GC}_{0})^{(g-11)}\big)\otimes\mathsf{S}_{16}\to\mathrm{gr}^{W}_{15}H^{k}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g}).

Corollary 7.4
.

The dimension of the compactly supported cohomology
H_{c}^{2g+k}(\mathcal{M}_{g})
grows at least exponentially with
g
for all
k\leq 73
with the possible exception of
k=1,4,7,71
.

This corollary was previously known for many, but not all, values of
k
in the stated range; see
[
15
, Corollary 1.2]
. The
21
new values of
k
are:

20,51,54,55,56,\dots,69,70,72,73.

Proof of Corollary
7.4
.

It is known that the dimension of
H^{2g+\kappa}(\mathsf{GC}_{0})^{(g)}
grows at least exponentially with
g
for
\kappa=0
and
\kappa=3
, by
[
8
]
and
[
14
, Proposition 2.4]
, respectively.
Furthermore,
H^{27}(\mathsf{GC}_{0})^{(10)}\cong\mathbb{Q}
by computer calculations.
Suppose we have an injection

H^{k-\delta}(\Sym^{p}(\mathsf{GC}_{0}))^{g-\delta^{\prime}}\to H^{k}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g}),

as asserted in the previous theorems for various values of
p
,
\delta
, and
\delta^{\prime}
.
Then
H^{2g+k}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g})
grows at least exponentially with
g
for any
k
of the form

\delta-2\delta^{\prime}+\kappa_{1}+\cdots+\kappa_{p},

where the
\kappa_{j}\in\{0,3,7\}
are such that at least one of them is in
\{0,3\}
and at most one of them is
7
.
The latter condition arises because the known cohomology in
H^{2g+7}(\mathsf{GC}_{0})^{(g)}
, namely
H^{27}(\mathsf{GC}_{0})^{(10)}\cong\mathbb{Q}
, is one-dimensional and concentrated in odd degree. Hence its higher symmetric powers vanish.
If
p\geq 2
, the resulting values of
k
are thus

\{\delta-2\delta^{\prime}+3j\mid j=0,\dots,p\}\cup\{\delta-2\delta^{\prime}+3j+7\mid j=0,\dots,p-1\}.

For example, consider the inclusion

H^{k-29}(\Sym^{14}(\mathsf{GC}_{0}))^{(g-1)}\to H_{c}^{k}(\mathcal{M}_{g})

from Corollary
7.3
. This provides at least exponential growth for
k
in the set

\{27,30,33,\dots,51,54,57,60,63,66,69\}\cup\{34,37,40,\dots,55,58,61,64,67,70,73\}.

Similarly, the other terms of Corollary
7.3
give at least exponential growth for
k
in the set:

\displaystyle\{26,29,\dots,68\}\ \cup\ \{33,36,\dots,72\}\ \cup\ \{24,27,\dots,63\}\ \cup\ \{31,34,\dots,67\}

\displaystyle\cup\

\displaystyle\{20,23,\dots,50\}\ \cup\ \{27,30,\dots,54\}\ \cup\ \{16,19,\dots,37\}\ \cup\ \{23,26,\dots,41\}

\displaystyle\cup\

\displaystyle\{12,15,\dots,24\}\ \cup\ \{17,20,\dots,26\}\ \cup\ \{8,11\}.

This then yields the list of Corollary
7.4
.
∎

8.
Euler characteristic of
\mathrm{gr}_{15,0}H^{*}_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})

The weight 11 Euler characteristic computation of
[
15
, Section 7]
, carries over to the type
(15,0)
, by replacing the truncation constant 10 with 14 and hence using
C_{g,n}^{15}
in place of the complex
C_{g,n}
in loc. cit. We just state the final result here.

Theorem 8.1
.

The equivariant Euler characteristic of the type
(15,0)
compactly supported cohomology of the moduli space of curves is computed by the following generating function:

\sum_{g,n\geq 0;\,2g+n\geq 3}u^{g+n}\chi_{\mathbb{S}_{n}}(\mathrm{gr}_{15,0}H_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n}))=\sum_{g,n}u^{g+n}\chi_{\mathbb{S}_{n}}(C^{15}_{g,n})\\
=-u\ T_{\leq 14}\bigg(\prod_{\ell\geq 1}\frac{U_{\ell}(\frac{1}{\ell}\sum_{d\mid\ell}\mu(\ell/d)(-p_{d}+1-w^{d}),u)}{U_{\ell}(\frac{1}{\ell}\sum_{d\mid\ell}\mu(\ell/d)(-p_{d}),u)}-1\bigg)\,,

where
T_{\leq 14}\left(\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{j}w^{j}\right):=\sum_{j=0}^{14}a_{j}
,

\displaystyle E_{\ell}

\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{\ell}\sum_{d\mid\ell}\mu(\ell/d)\frac{1}{u^{d}},

\displaystyle\lambda_{\ell}

\displaystyle:=u^{\ell}(1-u^{\ell})\ell,

\displaystyle B(z)

\displaystyle:=\sum_{r\geq 2}\frac{B_{r}}{r(r-1)}\frac{1}{z^{r-1}}

and
U_{\ell}(X,u)
is characterized by

\displaystyle\log U_{\ell}(X,u)

\displaystyle=\log\frac{(-\lambda_{\ell})^{X}\Gamma(-E_{\ell}+X)}{\Gamma(-E_{\ell})}

\displaystyle=X\left(\log(\lambda_{\ell}E_{\ell})-1\right)+(-E_{\ell}+X-\textstyle{\frac{1}{2}})\log(1-\textstyle{\frac{X}{E_{\ell}}})+B(-E_{\ell}+X)-B(-E_{\ell}).

We provide a computer generated table for small values of
(g,n)
in Figure
1
.

Remark 8.2
.

In
[
7
]
, we studied the asymptotic behavior of the weight 11 Euler characteristic
\chi(\mathrm{gr}_{11}H_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g}))
as
g\to\infty
.
Given that the formula for the type
(15,0)
Euler characteristic above is almost identical to the type
(11,0)
case (modulo the replacement of the constant 10 by 14 in the truncation operator
T_{\leq k}
), the analysis of loc. cit. also applies to the case above.
We hence find the asymptotic formula as
g\to\infty
:

\chi(\mathrm{gr}_{15,0}H_{c}(\mathcal{M}_{g}))\sim\begin{cases}D_{\infty}^{ev}\frac{(-1)^{g/2}(g-2)!}{(2\pi)^{g}}&\text{for $g$ even}\\
D_{\infty}^{odd}\frac{(-1)^{(g-1)/2}(g-2)!}{(2\pi)^{g}}&\text{for $g$ odd}\end{cases}

with the constants

\displaystyle D_{\infty}^{ev}

\displaystyle=-\sum_{j=8}^{\infty}\frac{(-4\pi^{2})^{j}}{j(2j-15)!14!}\approx 0.498203,\mbox{ and}

\displaystyle D_{\infty}^{odd}

\displaystyle=-\sum_{j=7}^{\infty}\frac{4\pi(-4\pi^{2})^{j}}{(2j+1)(2j-14)!14!}\approx 1.24975.
